title: Workspace
short_desc: The central problem-solving space holding four letter strings and all perceptual structures built during a run.
full_desc:
The Workspace is the central arena where Metacat's analogy-making unfolds. It contains four letter strings arranged in two rows: the top row holds the initial string and its modified counterpart (representing the given transformation, such as 'abc' to 'abd'), and the bottom row holds the target string and the answer string (the analogy to be discovered, such as 'xyz' to '?'). Every perceptual structure that Metacat builds during a run lives in the Workspace, and the interplay among these structures determines the system's evolving interpretation of the problem.

The Workspace holds six types of perceptual structures. Letters are the atomic elements, each positioned within its parent string. Descriptions attach semantic properties to objects, such as letter-category, string-position, length, and direction. Bonds represent relationships between adjacent objects along a particular facet -- for example, a successor bond on the letter-category facet between 'a' and 'b'. Groups are structured collections of letters or subgroups that share a common bond pattern, direction, and category. Bridges map objects across different strings, carrying concept-mappings that describe how one object's descriptions correspond to another's -- via identity, slippage, or coattail mappings. Rules are transformation descriptions that characterize how one string changes into another, built from the bridges that connect them.

Every structure in the Workspace passes through a lifecycle of three proposal levels: proposed, evaluated, and built. A scout codelet first proposes the structure, then an evaluator codelet assesses its strength, and finally a builder codelet promotes it to built status if it is strong enough. If the structure is too weak, it fizzles and is discarded. Built structures can also be broken later if a competing structure proves stronger, keeping the Workspace interpretation fluid.

Structure strength is a crucial concept. Each structure's strength is computed from two components: its internal coherence (how well its parts fit together) and its external support (how well it fits with other structures already in the Workspace). These values are recomputed every update cycle and feed into temperature calculation. Objects in the Workspace also have importance and salience values that determine how likely they are to be noticed by scout codelets, creating a form of emergent attention.

The Workspace is not a passive container but an active participant in the architecture's control loop. During each update cycle, the system spreads activation from the Workspace to the Themespace, recomputes structure strengths, update object salience, and recalculate temperature. The state of the Workspace thus continuously shapes which codelets get posted and how the system explores the problem space.

title: Slipnet (Semantic Network)
short_desc: A semantic network of 59 concept nodes whose activation levels enable fluid conceptual slippage during analogy-making.
full_desc:
The Slipnet is Metacat's long-term conceptual memory, implemented as a semantic network of 59 concept nodes connected by weighted links. Unlike the Workspace, which changes from run to run, the Slipnet's structure is fixed -- it represents the system's permanent knowledge about the letter-string domain. Nodes represent concepts such as individual letters (a through z), string positions (leftmost, rightmost, middle, whole, single), object categories (letter, group), bond types (sameness, successor, predecessor), directions (left, right), group categories (same-group, successor-group, predecessor-group), the two bond facets (letter-category and length), and small numbers (one through five).

Each Slipnet node has an activation level ranging from 0 to 100. Activation flows into the Slipnet from the Workspace: a structure activates the concepts it uses from the moment it is proposed, so a concept becomes relevant as soon as the run starts considering it (`bonds.ss:321`). Once activated, nodes spread activation to their neighbors along weighted links, and activation decays over time. A node passes the threshold at 50, which is when it drives top-down scouting, and is fully active at 100, which is when it spreads to its neighbours and begins to influence processing top-down -- for example, by causing top-down scout codelets to be posted that look for instances of that concept in the Workspace.

The most important property of the Slipnet is that it enables conceptual slippage, the key mechanism underlying fluid analogy. Slippage occurs when activation patterns cause normally-distinct concepts to be treated as interchangeable. For example, when the concept 'opposite' becomes highly active (perhaps because the problem involves a reversal), it can cause 'leftmost' and 'rightmost' to slip into each other, or 'successor' and 'predecessor' to swap. This is not a logical deduction but an emergent perceptual shift driven by activation dynamics. The degree of slippage depends on link weights and current activation levels, making it context-sensitive.

The Slipnet has five types of links: category links (connecting instances to their category, e.g., 'a' to 'letter-category'), instance links (the reverse), property links (connecting concepts to their properties), lateral links (connecting related concepts at the same level), and lateral-sliplinks (connecting concepts that can slip into each other, such as 'left' and 'right' via 'opposite'). Each node also has a conceptual depth value -- an intrinsic property indicating how abstract or fundamental the concept is. Deep concepts like 'opposite' and 'successor' resist decay more strongly than shallow concepts like individual letters, and drive top-down scouting with greater urgency once they are active, so a deep concept that becomes relevant stays relevant and shapes what the program looks for.

Slipnet nodes can be clamped -- held at full activation for a fixed period -- during initialization or during snag-response episodes. Clamping forces the system to attend to particular concepts, overriding the normal activation dynamics. This is used both at startup (to bootstrap relevant concepts) and during jootsing (to force exploration of alternative interpretations).

title: Coderack (Stochastic Scheduler)
short_desc: A stochastic scheduler that probabilistically selects from a pool of small specialized agents (codelets) to drive all processing.
full_desc:
The Coderack is Metacat's stochastic scheduler -- a pool of small, specialized agents called codelets that collectively drive all processing. There is no central controller in Metacat; instead, behavior emerges from the probabilistic selection and execution of many codelets, each performing a single micro-task. The Coderack can hold up to 100 codelets at any time, distributed across seven urgency levels: extremely-low, very-low, low, medium, high, very-high, and extremely-high.

Codelet selection is probabilistic and temperature-modulated. Each codelet's probability of being selected is proportional to its urgency level, but the degree to which urgency matters depends on the current temperature. At high temperature (the system is confused, little structure has been built), selection is nearly random -- all codelets have roughly equal chances regardless of urgency. At low temperature (strong structures exist, the system is confident), selection becomes greedy -- high-urgency codelets are strongly preferred. Together with staged structure-building -- every structure is scouted, then evaluated, then built, and can be abandoned at any stage -- this urgency-weighted stochastic selection implements what Hofstadter calls a 'parallel terraced scan': not true parallelism, but a probabilistic approximation in which many potential avenues are explored in proportion to their promise, each avenue getting further attention in proportion to how well it has done so far. Temperature modulates how sharply that scan focuses.

Metacat uses over 40 distinct codelet types, organized into several families. Scout codelets explore the Workspace for potential structures: bottom-up scouts notice salient objects, top-down scouts look for instances of highly-active Slipnet concepts, and thematic scouts pursue structures consistent with dominant Themespace patterns. Evaluator codelets assess proposed structures for strength and coherence. Builder codelets promote evaluated structures to built status, potentially fighting and breaking competing structures in the process. Breaker codelets remove weak structures. Rule codelets discover, evaluate, and translate transformation rules. Bridge codelets establish mappings between objects across strings. Progress-watcher codelets monitor whether the system is making forward progress. Jootser codelets detect and respond to repetitive failure patterns. Answer-justifier codelets validate proposed answers.

New codelets are posted to the Coderack during each update cycle (every 15 codelet executions). Bottom-up codelets are posted according to how unhappy the Workspace's objects are: unhappiness is collected into buckets, and the bucket a string falls into decides how many scouts it receives, so poorly accounted-for objects get explored. Top-down codelets are posted from eleven designated Slipnet nodes, each posting its own scouts once it is active, so the concepts that can direct a search are the ones that do. Thematic codelets are posted for the themes of a bridge type whose thematic pressure has been switched on by a clamp, biasing the system toward -- or, for a negative clamp, away from -- that interpretation. This continuous replenishment keeps the Coderack stocked with a mix of exploratory and focused agents.

A codelet pattern can be clamped by hand from this panel. A pattern is a set of codelet types pinned together at high urgency -- a scout at very-high alongside the evaluator and builder at extremely-high -- so that clamping one pins a whole line of work rather than a single type, and the structures that scout proposes actually get built. Five are offered: top-down, bottom-up, rule, bridge and group. Pressing a pattern clamps it and pressing it again releases it; clamping a second pattern releases the first. This is the third of Metacat's three manual clamp handles, beside Slipnet nodes and themes.\n\nThe Coderack's stochastic nature is fundamental to Metacat's design philosophy. By avoiding deterministic control, the system can explore unexpected avenues and discover creative analogies that a rigid controller would miss. The randomness is not noise -- it is a principled search strategy that balances exploration and exploitation through temperature regulation.

title: Themespace (Self-Watching)
short_desc: The self-watching mechanism that tracks activated thematic patterns across conceptual dimensions, enabling Metacat to monitor and influence its own perception.
full_desc:
The Themespace is Metacat's intermediate level of processing. Metacat's architecture has three levels: the subcognitive level, made up of the Workspace, the Slipnet and the Coderack; the intermediate level, which is the Themespace; and the cognitive level, which is the Temporal Trace, the focus for self-watching. Patterns of themes act as the medium through which the program wields control over its own behaviour, sitting above the subcognitive level and strongly influencing it, while the Trace holds the program's recent past. A theme pattern reflects Metacat's immediate experience -- its state of mind at that moment.

The Themespace works by tracking themes -- activated patterns along conceptual dimensions that characterize the perceptual interpretation being built at any moment. Copycat perceives patterns in its input data; Metacat additionally represents patterns in its own processing, and the Themespace is where those patterns live.

Themes are organized into clusters defined by two coordinates: a bridge type and a conceptual dimension. The three bridge types are one per mapping between the four strings: top-bridge (initial to modified), bottom-bridge (target to answer), and vertical-bridge (initial to target). Dimensions include direction, group-category, letter-category, bond-facet, string-position, and others. A theme within a cluster names the *relation* that a bridge's concept-mappings exhibit along that dimension for that bridge type -- identity, opposite, successor, predecessor, or different. A left-to-right mapping in the top bridge gives the theme 'top-bridge, Direction: identity'. A concept-mapping from a to x carries no relating concept between the two letters, so it gives the theme 'vertical-bridge, Letter-Category: different'. The concept-mapping belongs to one bridge; the theme is the pattern that many bridges can share.

There are 75 themes, arranged in 27 clusters. A cluster is one bridge type paired with one dimension, and there are nine dimensions: Letter-Category and Length each admit identity, successor, predecessor and different; String-Position, Bond-Category and Group-Category each admit identity, opposite and different; Alphabetic-Position and Direction each admit identity and opposite; Object-Category and Bond-Facet each admit identity and different. That is 25 themes per bridge type, and 75 in all. This follows the Metacat source, which builds a cluster for every Slipnet node carrying instance-links, Bond-Category among them. The dissertation states a total of 66 possible themes, counting the same nine dimensions with Bond-Category set aside; Petacat implements the source's 75.

Each theme carries one signed activation between -100 and +100. Positive means the theme supports its idea; negative means it opposes it; and there is no effective difference between a theme at zero and the theme not being in the Themespace at all. The sign says which side of its idea a theme is on, and it stays on that side under cluster dynamics: exciting a positive theme pushes it toward +100 and inhibiting it pulls it toward zero, while exciting a negative theme pushes it toward -100 and inhibiting it pulls it toward zero. A theme crosses from one side to the other when it is clamped. Themes interact within and across clusters through excitatory and inhibitory dynamics. Within a cluster, themes representing similar or compatible mappings excite each other, while themes representing opposing mappings inhibit each other. Across clusters, activation propagates when different bridge types share the same dimension and concept-mapping -- for example, if the top bridge maps direction left-to-right, this supports a similar mapping in the bottom bridge.

Dominance and thematic pressure are two separate things. A theme is dominant when it leads its cluster by more than a margin -- themes are ranked by absolute activation, and the leader must itself be positively activated. Dominance is a readout: the dominant themes of a bridge type form that bridge type's theme pattern, which is what characterizes a rule, what an answer description is indexed and compared by, and what justify mode unifies across the top and bottom string pairs. Most of the time themes are representational structures, a running commentary on the interpretation taking shape, and reading them off leaves the run unchanged.

Thematic pressure is switched on for a bridge type by clamping a theme pattern. A clamp pins each theme in the pattern at plus or minus 100, zeroes the rest of each affected dimension, freezes those clusters, and turns pressure on for that bridge type. While a bridge type is under pressure, thematic scout codelets are posted for its themes, and a slippage whose theme is dominant in its cluster counts as maximally important -- pressure and dominance both, not either alone. Four things clamp a pattern: a snag response, justify mode unifying its two rules, jootsing (which clamps the negative of a pattern that keeps failing), and a manual clamp from this panel. Those episodes are where self-watching feeds back into perception.

The Themespace also plays a critical role in answer characterization. When Metacat finds an answer, the dominant themes of each bridge type are distilled into three theme-patterns -- top, bottom and vertical -- and those patterns give a rich, multidimensional description of the interpretation that led to that answer. This thematic fingerprint is stored in Episodic Memory alongside the answer, enabling the system to compare answers not just by their surface form but by the deep perceptual patterns that produced them. Two different answers to the same problem will have different thematic profiles, allowing Metacat to explain why one interpretation is more compelling than another. Each theme carries two controls. **Clamp +100** pins it as positive thematic pressure, so the program favours structures compatible with that idea; **Clamp -100** pins it as negative pressure, so it favours structures incompatible with it, which is the manual counterpart of jootsing. A clamp zeroes the rest of that dimension, freezes the cluster, switches thematic pressure on for that bridge type, and records a manual-clamp event in the Trace. Pressing the control a theme already holds clears it. While pressure is on, **Release clamps** at the top of the panel frees every clamped theme at once and switches thematic pressure off, so the run goes back to building on evidence alone.

title: Temporal Trace
short_desc: A chronological event log recording all significant cognitive events during a run, enabling retrospective analysis of the system's processing history.
full_desc:
The Temporal Trace is Metacat's chronological record of all significant cognitive events that occur during a run. Seven kinds of event are recorded, each with a sequential event number, an event type, and references to the structures that existed at the time: a Slipnet concept becoming important enough to note, a slippage important enough to note, a group that matters to the interpretation, a rule discovered, a snag, a clamp, and an answer found. An event is recorded when it is important enough, which is what keeps the Trace short enough to reason over. The Trace provides Metacat with something Copycat entirely lacks: a memory of its own processing history.

The Trace is Metacat's cognitive level -- the focus for self-watching. Of the three levels of processing, the subcognitive level is the Workspace, the Slipnet and the Coderack; the intermediate level is the Themespace, whose theme patterns are the medium through which the program controls its own behaviour; and the cognitive level is the Trace, a short-term memory of recent past experience within a single run. A theme pattern says what the program's state of mind is now; the Trace says what has happened.

The Trace serves as the raw data source for Metacat's self-watching mechanisms. A snag event is recorded when applying a translated rule to the target string fails, and it carries the rule, the translation and the failure. Progress-watcher codelets read the Trace during a clamp period: once enough time has passed since the last event for the run to have settled, a progress-watcher lifts the clamp and posts an answer-finder with an urgency equal to the progress made. Jootser codelets go further, analyzing sequences of snag and clamp events to detect repetitive failure patterns -- cases where the run keeps arriving at the same impasse by the same route.

The Trace also supports Metacat's ability to reason about its own behavior after the fact. When an answer is found, the Trace is what the program's description of that answer is built from -- the themes and rules that produced it, the structures supporting them, the temperature at the moment of discovery, and any snags along the way. That description goes into Episodic Memory and outlives the run. When Metacat is asked to compare two answers, it retrieves the abstract descriptions of both from Episodic Memory and analyses the themes and rules they contain, sorting the themes into those the two answers hold in common, those that share a dimension but differ by relation, and those unique to one answer. The Trace is thus the source of what the program is later able to say about a run it has finished.

Each event in the Trace captures not just what happened but when it happened relative to other events. This ordering is essential for detecting temporal patterns. For example, a jootser codelet might notice that the system has built and then broken the same type of bond three times in the last 50 codelet steps, indicating that it is stuck in a loop. Without the temporal ordering provided by the Trace, such patterns would be invisible.

The Trace is reset at the beginning of each run, so it captures the processing history of a single problem-solving episode. Cross-run memory is handled by Episodic Memory, which stores compressed answer and snag descriptions rather than raw event sequences. Click an event to display it: the theme-pattern current at that moment is imposed over the live Themespace and the event is highlighted. Clicking it again restores the live state.

title: Episodic Memory
short_desc: A cross-run memory store that saves rich answer and snag descriptions, supporting reminding, comparison, and commentary across problem-solving episodes.
full_desc:
Episodic Memory is Metacat's persistent store of past problem-solving experiences, preserving rich descriptions of answers and snags across multiple runs. While the Workspace and Temporal Trace are reset at the beginning of each run, Episodic Memory accumulates over the system's lifetime, giving Metacat the ability to remember, compare, and learn from its previous analogies. This addresses one of the major weaknesses of Copycat, which treats every run as an isolated event with no memory of past results.

The primary unit stored in Episodic Memory is the answer description -- a structured characterization of a discovered answer that includes the problem strings, the answer string itself, the rules used to derive it (with abstractness ratings), the supporting bridges and concept-mappings, the three distilled theme-patterns at the time of discovery -- the dominant themes of the top, bottom and vertical bridges rather than the whole activation field, the temperature at which the answer was found, a quality score from 0 to 100, and any unjustified slippages (concept substitutions that were not supported by the built structures). Episodic Memory also stores snag descriptions that record failure episodes, capturing the themes and structures involved when the system got stuck.

Episodic Memory supports three key operations. Reminding occurs automatically when a new answer is found: the system compares the new answer's thematic profile against all stored answer descriptions, and any sufficiently similar past answers are reactivated, brought back to the system's attention. This is analogous to the human experience of being reminded of a past insight when encountering a similar situation. An answer description also carries three abstractness figures -- how abstract its top rule is, how abstract its bottom rule is, and how abstract its themes are on average. Metacat weighs two answers partly by these when it says which one it prefers, and the reason it gives names the criterion that decided it.\n\nThe similarity metric is a distance built from five factors: how many themes differ or are unique to one answer, how far apart the two answers' rules are structurally and conceptually, how far apart those rules are in abstractness, which themes are justified for one answer but not the other, and whether the two answers agree in coherence. Three of the five concern the rules, so an answer is remembered by what it did as much as by how it saw the problem. None of the factors reads the surface form of the strings, so the system can be reminded across different problems when the underlying conceptual patterns match.

Comparison allows two answers to be directly contrasted, analyzing their shared versus differing themes, rules, and supporting structures. This enables Metacat to articulate why one answer is better than another, or how two different answers to the same problem reflect different perceptual interpretations. The comparison mechanism works at the level of themes and concept-mappings, not raw strings, enabling deep structural comparison.

Commentary is the system's ability to generate natural-language English descriptions of answers and comparisons. This is not natural language understanding -- it is template-based transcription from the Slipnet concept vocabulary into English phrases. For example, Metacat can say 'The answer xyz was produced by replacing the rightmost letter by its successor' or 'Both answers share the theme of left-to-right directionality in their top bridges.' This commentary capability makes the system's reasoning accessible and interpretable.

Episodic Memory is the only thing that survives a run boundary. The Slipnet, the Themespace, the Workspace, the Coderack, the Temporal Trace, the temperature and the random stream are all rebuilt for each new run; the memory is handed on. That is what makes a sequence of runs a *training session* rather than a sequence of unrelated attempts, and it is why clearing the memory from the Admin view is what separates one session from the next. Every mode shares that memory: a Fast run inherits from the session and contributes to it exactly as Normal and Audit do. Each stored answer carries three actions. **display** re-enters that episode, imposing its vertical, top and bottom theme-patterns over the live Themespace, and again restores the live state. **explain** gives the program's own account of what the answer is based on. **forget** deletes that one answer, which is how you ask the program to look for it again.

title: Temperature
short_desc: A global control parameter (0-100) that serves as an inverse measure of problem organization and regulates the randomness of all stochastic decisions.
full_desc:
Temperature is a single global value ranging from 0 to 100 that serves as an inverse measure of how well Metacat has organized the current problem. It is computed from the quantity and quality of built structures in the Workspace and is updated every 15 codelet executions (each update cycle). Temperature is not merely a diagnostic -- it actively regulates the randomness of stochastic decisions throughout the system, functioning as the master control knob for the exploration-exploitation tradeoff.

At high temperature (near 100), little structure has been built and the system is in a state of high uncertainty. Codelet selection from the Coderack becomes nearly random, with urgency levels having little effect on selection probability. This allows broad, unfocused exploration of the problem space, giving weak or unlikely ideas a chance to be pursued. Structure-building decisions are also more random at high temperature -- the system is more willing to accept weak structures and less likely to break existing ones. High temperature characterizes the early stages of a run, before the system has formed any coherent interpretation.

At low temperature (near 0), strong structures have been built and the system is confident in its interpretation. Codelet selection becomes greedy, with high-urgency codelets strongly preferred over low-urgency ones. Structure-building is more discriminating -- only strong structures survive, and weak competitors are readily broken. Low temperature characterizes the later stages of a run, when the system is converging on an answer and refining its interpretation.

Temperature can be clamped -- held at a fixed value -- during snag-response periods. A snag sets the temperature to 100 and clamps it there, so the run explores broadly from the impasse. By preventing temperature from dropping, clamping ensures that the system continues to explore rather than prematurely converging on an inadequate interpretation. The clamp is released stochastically, with a probability equal to the progress made since the snag, so a snag period ends as soon as the program starts building again and persists while it does not.

Temperature is a weighted average of two quantities, 70 percent the Workspace's average unhappiness and 30 percent a rule factor. Average unhappiness aggregates how poorly accounted for each object is, so it falls as bonds, groups and bridges take hold. The rule factor is binary: it is 0 once a rule is both possible and supported for the top string pair -- and, in justify mode, for the bottom pair as well -- and 100 otherwise. Because the rule factor contributes 30 points on its own, a Workspace whose objects are entirely happy sits at about 30 until a supported rule exists, and reaches the low single digits once one does. Temperature therefore measures two things at once: how well the strings are organised, and whether the program has an account of the transformation. This creates a natural feedback loop: as the system builds better structures, temperature drops, making the system more focused, which in turn helps it build even better structures -- until it converges on an answer or encounters a snag.

title: Codelet
short_desc: A small, specialized agent that performs a single micro-task during one step of Metacat's processing.
full_desc: Codelets are the fundamental units of computation in Metacat. Each codelet is a small procedure focused on one specific micro-task, such as looking for a potential bond between two adjacent letters, evaluating a proposed group's strength, or attempting to build a bridge between objects in different strings. Codelets are stored in the Coderack and selected probabilistically for execution. For example, a 'bond-scout' codelet might notice that letters 'a' and 'b' are adjacent and propose a successor bond between them. Over 40 distinct codelet types exist, organized into families: scouts, evaluators, builders, breakers, rule codelets, bridge codelets, progress-watchers, jootsers, and answer-justifiers.

title: Slippage
short_desc: A conceptual substitution where one concept is fluidly replaced by a related concept during analogy-making.
full_desc: Slippage is the mechanism by which Metacat achieves fluid, creative analogies rather than rigid structural mappings. When activation patterns in the Slipnet cause normally-distinct concepts to become interchangeable, a slippage occurs. For example, in the problem 'abc -> abd; xyz -> ?', the concept 'leftmost' may slip to 'rightmost' via the 'opposite' link, enabling the system to see 'z' (the rightmost letter) as analogous to 'c' (the rightmost letter) rather than 'x' (the leftmost). Slippages are carried by concept-mappings in bridges and are central to how Metacat produces answers like 'xyd' instead of the literal 'xya'.

title: Bond
short_desc: A relationship between two adjacent objects in a string, characterized by a bond category and bond facet.
full_desc: A bond represents a perceived relationship between two neighboring objects (letters or groups) within the same string. Each bond has a category (sameness, successor, or predecessor) and a facet (letter-category, length, alphabetic-position, or direction) that specifies along which dimension the relationship holds. For example, 'a' and 'b' can be connected by a successor bond on the letter-category facet, meaning 'b' is the successor of 'a' in the alphabet. Bonds are the building blocks of groups -- a sequence of same-category bonds in the same direction can be chunked into a group.

title: Bridge
short_desc: A mapping between objects in different strings, carrying concept-mappings that describe how their descriptions correspond.
full_desc: A bridge connects objects across two different strings, establishing a correspondence that is central to analogy-making. Each bridge carries one or more concept-mappings that describe how the descriptions of the two objects relate. Bridges come in three types, one per mapping between the four strings: horizontal-top (initial to modified), horizontal-bottom (target to answer), and vertical (initial to target). For example, a vertical bridge might map the 'c' in 'abc' to the 'z' in 'xyz', with a concept-mapping of 'rightmost -> rightmost' (identity) or 'leftmost -> rightmost' (slippage via opposite).

title: Rule
short_desc: A transformation description that characterizes how one string changes into another, built from bridges and measured by quality.
full_desc: A rule describes the transformation from one string to another, capturing both what changed and at what level of abstraction. A rule clause is one of three kinds. An intrinsic clause describes a change to a single object, such as 'replace the rightmost letter by its successor'. An extrinsic clause describes attributes exchanged among a set of objects, such as 'swap the positions of the leftmost and rightmost letters'. A verbatim clause gives a new sequence of letters outright, which is how a change that resists description is still expressed. Rule quality is measured along three dimensions: uniformity (consistency of the concept-mappings), abstractness (how deep the concepts used are), and succinctness (how compactly the rule can be stated). Rules are the structures that get translated across strings to produce answers.

title: Theme
short_desc: An activated pattern along a conceptual dimension in the Themespace, characterizing an aspect of the current interpretation.
full_desc: A theme represents an activated conceptual pattern within the Themespace, organized by bridge type and dimension. Themes capture the character of the interpretation being built -- for example, 'in the top bridge, the direction dimension shows a left-to-right identity mapping.' Each theme carries one signed activation between -100 and +100 -- positive for supporting its idea, negative for opposing it, zero for having no bearing -- and themes within a cluster compete through excitatory and inhibitory interactions that move a theme toward its own pole or toward zero. A theme is dominant when it leads its cluster by more than a margin, which makes it part of that bridge type's theme pattern -- the pattern that characterizes rules and indexes answers in memory. Thematic pressure, which biases codelet posting and structure evaluation toward an interpretation, is switched on separately by clamping a theme pattern: during a snag response, during justify mode, during jootsing, or by hand from the Themespace panel.

title: Snag
short_desc: A failure to apply a translated rule to the target string, recorded in the Trace with the rule and the failure, and stored in Episodic Memory.
full_desc:
A snag is a failure to apply a translated rule to the target string. Metacat translates the rule it found for the top string pair into the target's terms and then applies it; a snag is the moment that application cannot be carried out. The canonical case is 'abc -> abd; xyz -> ?', where the rule asks for the successor of the rightmost letter and z has none. Three kinds arise: a swap, where objects exchange attributes in a way the target cannot hold; a conflict, where two demands on the string disagree; and a change, where an object is asked to become something it cannot be.

A snag names the rule that ran aground, the translated rule, the bridges supporting the translation and the slippages taken along the way, so it is a specific account of an impasse rather than a report that progress has stopped. That account is what a snag description in Episodic Memory is built from (§4.7.2), and what lets a later answer be recognised as one that avoids the impasse.

When a snag is recorded, the system discards every proposed bond, group and bridge, sets temperature to 100 and clamps it there, clamps the theme-pattern of the interpretation that ran aground, empties the Coderack, and posts the initial codelets afresh. The run restarts its perceptual work from the strings while holding on to what it has built and to the themes that characterise the failure. Repeated snags with overlapping themes trigger the jootsing mechanism. For example, if the system repeatedly tries and fails to translate a rule because the target string lacks a required letter, a snag records this pattern so jootsing can inhibit the stuck interpretation.

title: Jootsing
short_desc: "Jumping Out Of The System" -- a meta-strategy for detecting and escaping repetitive failure patterns.
full_desc: Jootsing (an acronym for 'Jumping Out Of The System,' coined by Douglas Hofstadter) is Metacat's meta-level strategy for breaking out of unproductive processing loops. When jootser codelets detect that the system has encountered repeated snags with overlapping thematic patterns, they analyze the common themes of the failures and clamp negative activation on those themes, actively inhibiting the stuck interpretation. This forces the system to explore alternative perspectives. For example, if the system keeps failing while trying to map strings left-to-right, jootsing might inhibit the left-to-right theme, opening up the possibility of a right-to-left mapping. If all alternatives are exhausted, the system may give up on the problem.

title: Clamping
short_desc: Holding a node, theme, or the temperature at a fixed value for a period, so a chosen idea governs what the run explores.
full_desc: Clamping is the act of freezing a value -- whether a Slipnet node's activation, a Themespace theme's activation, or the global temperature -- at a fixed level for a defined number of codelet steps or update cycles. During initialization, relevant Slipnet nodes are clamped at full activation for a warm-up period to bootstrap the system. During a snag response the temperature is set to 100 and clamped there, which makes codelet selection maximally random and sends the run exploring broadly away from the impasse; it is released stochastically, in proportion to the progress made since. During jootsing, negative theme activation may be clamped to inhibit a stuck interpretation. Clamping overrides normal activation dynamics and is temporary: a Slipnet clamp expires after its warm-up period, and a snag's temperature clamp lifts in proportion to progress.

title: Temperature (Glossary)
short_desc: A global randomness parameter ranging from 0 (deterministic, confident) to 100 (chaotic, confused).
full_desc: Temperature is a global value (0 to 100) that inversely measures how well the system has organized the problem. It is computed from the quantity and quality of built structures and updated every 15 codelets. High temperature (near 100) means little structure exists, so the system explores broadly with near-random codelet selection. Low temperature (near 0) means strong structures are in place, so selection becomes greedy and focused. Temperature regulates all stochastic decisions in the system, implementing the exploration-exploitation tradeoff.

title: Salience
short_desc: A measure of how attention-worthy an object is, combining its importance and unhappiness values.
full_desc: Salience determines how likely a Workspace object is to be noticed and acted upon by scout codelets. It is computed as a combination of the object's importance (based on how many descriptions, bonds, and bridges it participates in) and its unhappiness (inversely related to how well it is integrated into the current interpretation). Intra-string salience weights unhappiness 80% and importance 20%, so lonely objects attract within-string attention. Inter-string salience inverts this (importance 80%, unhappiness 20%), so well-described objects attract cross-string mapping attention. An isolated letter with no bonds would have high unhappiness and thus high intra-string salience, making it a likely target for bottom-up scouts.

title: Activation
short_desc: The current activity level (0-100) of a Slipnet node or Themespace theme, determining its influence on processing.
full_desc: Activation is a numeric value (0 to 100) assigned to each Slipnet node and Themespace theme, representing how relevant or active that concept currently is. Activation flows into the Slipnet from the Workspace when built structures use a concept, spreads along weighted links to neighboring nodes, and decays over time. Deeper concepts decay more slowly than shallow ones. A node at 50 or above is *above threshold*, which is what lets it post top-down codelets; a node is *fully active* only at exactly 100, which is what lets it spread to its neighbours, shrink its links, and count its descriptions and concept-mappings as relevant. Between 50 and 100 a node may jump to full activation, with probability the cube of its activation. For example, if many successor bonds are built, the 'successor' node's activation rises, causing top-down scouts to look for more successor relationships.

title: Conceptual Depth
short_desc: An intrinsic property of each Slipnet node indicating how abstract or fundamental the concept is.
full_desc: Conceptual depth is a fixed numeric property (0-100) of each Slipnet node that measures how abstract, fundamental, or 'deep' the concept is. Shallow concepts like individual letters have low conceptual depth (around 10); their activation decays quickly and they drive top-down scouting weakly. Deep concepts like 'opposite' and 'identity' have high conceptual depth (around 90); their activation decays slowly and they post top-down codelets at higher urgency, so they exert greater influence on processing. Conceptual depth also factors into rule quality: rules that use deeper concepts (like 'replace the rightmost letter by its successor') are rated as more abstract and higher-quality than rules using shallow concepts (like 'replace c by d').

title: Spanning Group
short_desc: A group that encompasses an entire string, treating the whole string as a single structured unit.
full_desc: A spanning group is a group whose members collectively cover every position in a string, effectively chunking the entire string into one structured object. For example, in the string 'abc', if all three letters are bonded by successor bonds and grouped together, the result is a spanning group of type 'successor-group' with direction 'right'. Spanning groups always have 100% external strength and are significant because they enable the system to describe and manipulate entire strings as single units, leading to more abstract and powerful rules. They are also important for bridge-building, since a spanning group can be mapped to a spanning group in another string.

title: Proposal Level
short_desc: The lifecycle stage of a Workspace structure: proposed, evaluated, or built.
full_desc: Every structure in the Workspace passes through three proposal levels during its lifecycle. A structure begins as 'proposed' when a scout codelet first suggests it. It advances to 'evaluated' when an evaluator codelet assesses its strength. Finally, it reaches 'built' when a builder codelet successfully promotes it, at which point it becomes part of the active Workspace interpretation. Structures can fizzle at the evaluation stage if they are too weak, or be broken after building if a stronger competing structure displaces them. Built structures are what contribute to temperature and generate Themespace themes. Slipnet concepts are activated from the proposal onward, so a concept is relevant while the structure using it is still being weighed.

title: Workspace Structure
short_desc: Any perceptual entity built in the Workspace: bonds, groups, bridges, descriptions, or rules.
full_desc: A workspace structure is the general term for any perceptual entity that exists in the Workspace. The six types are: letters (atomic elements), descriptions (semantic properties attached to objects), bonds (relationships between adjacent objects), groups (structured collections of objects), bridges (mappings across strings), and rules (transformation descriptions). All structures except letters share a common lifecycle (proposed -> evaluated -> built), have computed strength values combining internal coherence and external support, and can be broken by competing structures. The set of built structures at any moment defines the system's current interpretation of the problem.

title: Concept Mapping
short_desc: A correspondence between two descriptions carried by a bridge, indicating identity, slippage, or coattail relationship.
full_desc: A concept-mapping is a correspondence between a description on one object and a description on another, carried by a bridge that connects them across strings. Concept-mappings come in three types: identity (the same concept maps to itself, e.g., 'rightmost -> rightmost'), slippage (one concept maps to a related but different concept, e.g., 'leftmost -> rightmost' via the opposite relation), and coattail (a mapping that follows from other mappings rather than being independently motivated). Concept-mapping strength rewards conceptual depth while slippability penalizes it, meaning deep identity mappings are very strong and deep slippages are very hard to achieve.

title: Description
short_desc: A semantic property attached to a Workspace object, pairing a description type with a descriptor from the Slipnet.
full_desc: A description is a semantic label attached to a Workspace object (letter or group) that identifies one of its properties. Each description pairs a description type (such as letter-category, string-position, or object-category) with a descriptor (the actual Slipnet concept, such as 'a', 'leftmost', or 'letter'). For example, the letter 'a' at the start of string 'abc' would have descriptions including (letter-category: a), (string-position: leftmost), and (object-category: letter). Descriptions are the basis for concept-mappings in bridges -- when a bridge connects two objects, it maps their descriptions to each other. A description is considered relevant when its type is fully active in the Slipnet.

title: Bond Facet
short_desc: The conceptual dimension along which a bond relationship is defined: letter-category, length, alphabetic-position, or direction.
full_desc: A bond facet specifies which conceptual dimension a bond relationship is measured along. The four bond facets are: letter-category (the identity of letters, e.g., 'a' succeeded by 'b'), length (the size of groups, e.g., a group of 2 succeeded by a group of 3), alphabetic-position (the numeric position in the alphabet), and direction (the directionality of groups). When a bond-scout codelet examines two adjacent objects, it checks each facet for potential sameness, successor, or predecessor relationships. Letter-category bonds tend to have higher internal strength than length bonds.

title: Group Category
short_desc: The classification of a group based on the bond type shared by its members: same-group, successor-group, or predecessor-group.
full_desc: A group category describes the type of internal regularity that defines a group. The three categories are: same-group (all internal bonds are sameness bonds, e.g., the group 'aaa'), successor-group (all internal bonds are successor bonds, e.g., the group 'abc'), and predecessor-group (all internal bonds are predecessor bonds, e.g., the group 'cba'). The group category, along with the bond facet and direction, fully characterizes the group's structure. For example, 'abc' is a successor-group on the letter-category facet with rightward direction.

title: Bond Category
short_desc: The type of relationship a bond represents: sameness, successor, or predecessor.
full_desc: Bond category classifies the relationship that a bond represents between two adjacent objects. The three categories are: sameness (the two objects are identical along the bond facet, e.g., 'a' and 'a'), successor (the right/second object follows the left/first along the bond facet, e.g., 'a' followed by 'b'), and predecessor (the right/second object precedes the left/first, e.g., 'b' followed by 'a'). Sameness has high conceptual depth (around 80), making sameness-based structures more abstract and resistant to decay than successor or predecessor bonds (depth around 50).

title: Direction
short_desc: The orientation of a group or bond sequence within a string: left or right.
full_desc: Direction indicates the orientation of a group or sequence of bonds within a string. A group with direction 'right' reads naturally from left to right (e.g., 'abc' as a rightward successor-group), while a group with direction 'left' reads from right to left (e.g., 'cba' as a leftward successor-group, since reading right-to-left yields a, b, c -- a successor sequence). Sameness bonds have no direction. Direction is one of the Slipnet concepts that commonly participates in slippage: 'left' and 'right' are connected by the 'opposite' link, so in problems involving reversal, direction slippage is a key mechanism for discovering the analogy.

title: Urgency
short_desc: A codelet's priority level (one of seven bins) that influences its probability of being selected from the Coderack.
full_desc: Urgency is a discrete priority level assigned to each codelet when it is posted to the Coderack. The seven urgency bins are: extremely-low, very-low, low, medium, high, very-high, and extremely-high (with numeric values 7, 21, 35, 49, 63, 77, and 91 respectively). Higher urgency increases a codelet's probability of being selected, but the effect is modulated by temperature -- at high temperature, urgency matters little (selection is nearly random), while at low temperature, urgency strongly biases selection (high-urgency codelets dominate). Urgency is typically set based on the strength of the structure the codelet is meant to act on, or the activation of the Slipnet concept that triggered it.

title: Update Cycle
short_desc: A periodic maintenance step occurring every 15 codelet executions that recomputes strengths, activation, temperature, and posts new codelets.
full_desc: An update cycle is a periodic maintenance step that occurs every 15 codelet executions. During an update cycle, the system: (a) recomputes all structure strengths in the Workspace, (b) updates object importance and salience values, (c) spreads activation from the Workspace to the Themespace through the built bridges, (d) spreads activation within the Themespace and then updates the Slipnet, (e) recomputes temperature, (f) posts new bottom-up and top-down codelets to the Coderack, and (g) updates graphical displays. The update cycle is the heartbeat of Metacat's control loop, synchronizing all components of the architecture.

title: Seeds and Stochastic Behaviour
short_desc: Petacat is stochastic by design: a different-but-correct run is right behaviour. A seed narrows that variation for development, and only while nothing the system has learned has changed.
full_desc:
Petacat is a stochastic system by design. Codelet selection, structure-building fights, and probabilistic choices are all driven by a pseudorandom number generator, and that randomness is the mechanism -- the parallel terraced scan explores many possible interpretations in proportion to how promising they look. Two runs of the same problem that reach the same answer by different routes are both correct, and so are two runs that reach different valid answers. Variation is not a defect to be engineered away.

Supplying the same random seed narrows that variation, which is useful while developing and debugging, and the dissertation's sample runs publish their seeds for that reason. But it is a development aid rather than a property of the architecture, and it is narrower than it looks: a seed only pins a run against an unchanged configuration -- the same slipnet, the same codelet definitions, the same parameters. Change any of them and the same seed produces a different run, correctly.

That limit matters because Petacat is built to grow beyond Metacat. Once the system learns -- adding concepts and connections to its own slipnet and carrying them forward -- its configuration is no longer fixed between runs, so reproducing an earlier run becomes progressively less possible and less meaningful. A learning system that repeated itself exactly would not be learning. What is worth preserving instead is the ability to inspect what a run did: saved run state and recorded processing history let a run be re-examined step by step whether or not it could ever be reproduced.

Four things narrow the seed further. Episodic Memory carries answers across the runs of a Training Session, and a run declines an answer the memory already holds for the same problem and the same rules, so repeating a problem within a session explores a different answer each time. Random numbers come from counter-based per-codelet streams, so a seed pins a run against the current stream layout. Running codelets in parallel makes a run unrepeatable, because the order in which they commit is unjournaled -- where a specific run needs explaining, re-run it in Audit mode, which is serial and records everything. And the GPU numeric backend computes in float32 where the reference computes in float64, which flips some probabilistic choices.

None of that is a loss of rigour, because the standard Petacat is actually held to is not "the same seed gives the same run". It is that the *set* of answers a problem can reach is unchanged -- membership, not frequency, and not a particular run. That set was established by sampling each of thirteen problems until no new answers were appearing (410,000 runs in total), and every change to the execution machinery is checked against it. A seeded run remains a convenience for development; the reachable set is the thing that is defended.

What has replaced exact repetition is re-execution. A Normal run records the complete state of the system at its start and at its end, so it can be reloaded and run again from exactly where it began -- which is a stronger guarantee than a seed, because it captures the episodic memory the run inherited as well as the problem it was given.

title: Persistence Mode (Fast, Normal, Audit)
short_desc: What a run writes down. Chosen when the run is created, fixed for its life, and deliberately unable to change what the engine computes.
full_desc:
Every run is created in one of three persistence modes, chosen in the Recording group of the Run Controls panel or by passing 'mode' when creating a run through the API. The mode says what is written down. It says nothing about what the engine computes, and that separation is enforced rather than merely intended: the engine emits the same events in the same order in every mode and is never told which one is in force, so there is no code path that could make a Fast run think differently from an Audit one.

**Normal** is the default. The complete state of the system is captured at the start of the run and again at its end, and nothing in between. That is enough to compare where a run began with where it finished, and enough to re-execute it: reload the recorded start state, run again, and the recorded end state follows. Complete state rather than just the problem and the seed, because a run inherits the episodic memory of everything before it, so the problem and the seed do not on their own determine what it does.

**Audit** records every state-changing action as a forward log, which is what the Review view's step-through inspector reads. It is deliberately serial -- one codelet at a time -- and takes roughly 1.8 times as long as Fast. Audit is also the permanent reference: a fully-recorded serial execution is what everything faster or more parallel is checked against.

**Fast** records nothing, ever. It never opens a database connection, not even to insert the row that would name it, so a Fast run completes with the database stopped. It has no run number to take from the database either and uses a negative one instead. It gets a throwaway episodic memory and discards its commentary as it goes. Nothing is buffered for later: the alternative reading of "fast" -- collect it all in memory and write it at the end -- is exactly what this mode is defined not to do. The cost is that a Fast run is absent from Run History and from Review, which is the mode working rather than a fault.

Measured on the same problem and seed, the three produce the same number of codelets and the same answer. Normal takes about 1.4 times as long as Fast and writes 137 KB; Audit takes about 1.8 times as long and writes 381 KB.

title: Training Session
short_desc: A sequence of runs sharing one episodic memory -- the only thing that crosses a run boundary.
full_desc:
A run is one letter-analogy problem plus Petacat's response. A training session is a sequence of runs that share one episodic memory, and that memory is the only thing that carries from one run to the next: the Slipnet, the Themespace, the Workspace, the Coderack, the Temporal Trace, the temperature and the random stream are all rebuilt for every run, exactly as in the original Metacat.

That is why the session is worth naming. It is the unit over which the system accumulates anything -- the span within which one run can be reminded of another. Clearing episodic memory from the Admin view is what separates one session from the next, because after a clear no run inherits anything from the runs before it.

Sessions are not something you create. One is opened automatically when a run needs one, and the runs that follow join it. The Review view lists sessions with their runs, so a session can be read back as the sequence it was. A run created in Fast mode is not part of any session: it uses its own throwaway memory and writes no row.

A session may mix all three persistence modes freely. Because the mode changes only what is recorded, a session of mixed modes is cognitively identical to the same session run entirely in Fast.

title: Numeric Substrate
short_desc: The engine's array arithmetic -- activation spreading, salience, structure strengths, themespace dynamics, temperature -- executed on the GPU through Metal.
full_desc:
Some of what Petacat does is decisions over structures: which object to look at, whether to build a bond, which codelet to run next. The rest is numbers over arrays: spreading activation across the Slipnet and decaying it, recomputing every object's importance and salience, recomputing every structure's strength, running the Themespace's excite-and-inhibit dynamics, and recalculating temperature. That second part is the numeric substrate, and it is written as flat arrays rather than as loops over the object graph so that it can be executed somewhere other than the Python interpreter.

Four implementations sit behind one interface: a pure-Python reference that is always available and defines what "correct" means, a vectorised CPU implementation in NumPy, and two through MLX -- one on the GPU's Metal cores and one on MLX's CPU stream. The three double-precision implementations agree with the reference exactly, down to the same number of random draws. The GPU is single-precision, because Metal has no double precision, so it genuinely makes some probabilistic choices differently and its runs diverge onto different answers. The set of answers reachable is unchanged, which is the standard that matters.

By default the GPU is used at every Slipnet size, and today that costs speed rather than saving it: a Metal dispatch takes about 0.2 milliseconds whether it is handed 200 connections or 340,000, and today's Slipnet has 59 concepts and 202 links, so the engine runs roughly eight to nine times slower with the substrate engaged than without it. The point is what comes next. The Slipnet is intended to grow toward hundreds of thousands of concepts, at which scale spreading activation is the dominant cost and the GPU is an order of magnitude ahead; the crossover is around ten thousand nodes. Running the GPU path now means it is exercised and correct before the Slipnet grows into it, rather than a code path nothing has ever executed.

title: Admin
short_desc: Destructive administrative operations: clear episodic memory, or fully reset all run data.
full_desc:
The Admin view is accessed from the hamburger menu and houses destructive operations that would be dangerous to place alongside everyday controls.

Clear Episodic Memory removes all stored answer and snag descriptions that Metacat has accumulated from past runs. After clearing, the engine can no longer 'remember' previous answers or get reminded of similar problems -- each subsequent run starts fresh. This does not affect the current run, run history, or any engine configuration. Useful when you want the system to approach a problem without bias from prior solutions.

Full Reset (delete everything) completely resets Petacat to its initial state. It stops any running engine, deletes every run and its history, clears episodic memory, and resets all UI panels. Database seed data (slipnet nodes, codelet types, engine parameters, demo problems, and other configuration) is preserved -- only user-created run data is destroyed.

Both actions require confirmation and cannot be undone. See the Admin panel itself for the exact API endpoints called and the detailed technical notes for each operation.

title: Free-Running
short_desc: Codelets executing simultaneously across CPU cores with no global barrier, with a lost race resolving as an ordinary fizzle.
full_desc:
Metacat's control loop is serial: choose a codelet, run it, repeat, with a housekeeping update every fifteen codelets. Free-running keeps the same architecture but lets several codelets execute at once on different CPU cores, with no barrier that everything has to stop at. Set the Workers box in Run Controls above 1 to run this way; it accepts 1 to 16, and an Audit run holds it at 1. Free-running is deliberately built as a wrapper around the serial runner, so the serial reference cannot acquire concurrency bugs by proximity.

The obvious objection is that a codelet then decides on a Workspace that has moved on by the time it acts. The architecture already has an answer: a codelet that loses a race *fizzles*, which is exactly what it does when the structure it proposed turns out too weak. Nothing new has to be invented for the model to interpret, and a rising fizzle rate reads correctly as the Workspace being busy. So most of the work is in *detecting* the situation: each codelet records what it read and the version each thing carried when it read it, and at the moment it commits, a read-set whose versions have all held is a codelet whose premises did not move.

How much staleness the architecture tolerates was measured before any of the concurrency was written, by making the serial loop read state as it stood N codelets ago. Nothing changes up to five codelets of lag; by fifteen, runs start taking longer to converge; by fifty, a genuinely new answer appears. Five is therefore the budget the parallel scheduler is tuned to stay inside.

Two things stay serial on purpose. The housekeeping update is not stopped for -- whichever worker reaches the boundary runs it while the others carry on. Committing a structure is serialised, because deciding a fight between two structures is a read-then-modify sequence over shared lists, and running two of those at once corrupts the lists rather than producing a conflict the model could read as a fizzle.

The practical consequence for a user is that a free-running run cannot be replayed afterwards: no record is kept of the order in which codelets committed. Where a specific run needs explaining, re-run it in Audit mode, which is serial and records everything.

title: Problem Input
short_desc: The four letter strings that define an analogy problem: Initial, Modified, Target, and (optionally) Answer.
full_desc:
The Problem Input panel is where you specify the analogy problem Metacat will attempt to solve. Every problem has the form 'Initial -> Modified; Target -> ?'. For example, 'abc -> abd; xyz -> ?' asks Metacat to find an analogous transformation for xyz given that abc became abd.

The four fields are:

- Initial: The starting string of the top row, e.g. 'abc'. This is what the transformation begins with.
- Modified: The result of the top-row transformation, e.g. 'abd'. Metacat will discover rules that describe how Initial became Modified.
- Target: The starting string of the bottom row, e.g. 'xyz'. Metacat will try to apply an analogous transformation to this string.
- Answer (optional): If you supply this, Metacat enters justification mode and tries to explain why this specific answer is (or isn't) a good analogy, rather than discovering an answer from scratch.

Seed sets the random seed. The same problem, the same seed and the same Episodic Memory reproduce a run exactly; blank or 0 means seed 0. It lives here because it is part of the problem's identity -- changing it gives you a different run of the same strings.

The Demo Problem dropdown lets you load pre-configured problems from the dissertation, including well-known examples like the 'abc -> abd; xyz -> ?' problem and many harder variations. Each demo also carries a preset seed, which pins the run while the configuration is unchanged -- handy for following a known-good run.

There are two different things you might mean by 'run it again', and they are separate controls:
- Edit any field (or pick another demo) and press Run in the Run Controls panel: this starts a NEW run on the new problem, leaving the previous one in the run history. The line under the Run button warns you when the inputs have drifted away from the run currently on screen.
- 'Reset to codelet 0' at the bottom of this panel: this clears the workspace of the CURRENT run back to bare strings, keeping the same problem and seed, so you can replay or retry it. It does not start running -- press Run afterwards. It works in every recording mode, including Fast, whose problem and seed are held by the running engine.

Problem Input fields are disabled while a run is in progress; press Stop first.

title: Run Controls
short_desc: Controls for starting, stepping, stopping, and configuring engine runs. Organized into Run, Recording, Manual stepping, and Settings groups.
full_desc:
The Run Controls panel decides *how* a run executes; the Problem Input panel above it decides *what* is run. It has four grouped sections:

**Run**: 'How to run' selects between the two mutually exclusive execution strategies; the button and the pacing control below it follow that choice.
- *Run to answer -- full speed*: the engine runs flat out on the backend until an answer is found (or an internal limit is reached). The Workspace panel header shows a spinner and a STOP button, and the UI samples the running engine at the Sampling Interval. 0 means continuous (~100ms); dragging right samples less often for lower UI overhead. This interval changes only how often the UI reads the engine, never how the engine runs. Use this when you want fast time-to-answer and don't need to see every codelet.
- *Live updates -- codelet by codelet*: the client drives one codelet at a time and refreshes every panel after each, so you can watch structures being built in real time. Delay Per Codelet inserts a pause after each one -- raise it to follow the run by eye. Much slower than full speed.
Stop halts whichever strategy is running. The line under the button names the run currently on screen, and warns when the problem in the inputs has drifted away from it -- in that case running starts a NEW run rather than continuing the old one.

**Recording**: 'What the run writes down' selects the run's persistence mode -- Normal, Audit or Fast. This is a genuinely different question from the one above it, and the two are placed side by side because they are the pair most easily confused: the execution strategy decides how this browser watches a run, while the persistence mode decides whether the run is written down at all.
- *Normal* (the default): the complete state of the system is captured at the start of the run and again at its end, and nothing in between. Enough to compare where a run began with where it finished, and enough to re-execute it.
- *Audit*: every state-changing action is recorded as a forward log, which is what the Review view's step-through inspector reads. It runs serially and takes roughly 1.8 times as long.
- *Fast*: nothing is recorded, ever. No database row, so no entry in Run History and nothing in Review, no contribution to episodic memory, and a negative run number because there is no row to take a positive one from. Useful for rapid iteration where the run itself is the point and the record is not.
The mode is fixed when a run is created, so choosing a different one starts a new run. None of the three changes what the engine computes: the same problem and seed give the same answer in all three, because the engine is never told which mode is in force.

**Manual stepping**: Step N executes exactly N codelets and stops, independently of both selectors above, so you can advance in small inspectable increments.

**Settings**: Configuration that affects how the engine runs:
- Spreading threshold: A fundamental parameter -- it changes what a run does. A run being stepped reports itself as running while each batch of codelets executes and paused between batches, waiting for the next request; a batch that reaches an answer reports the answer. The engine pushes that status, the codelet count and the temperature as they change, so the display follows the run without asking for it.\n\nThe slider reports the threshold of the run on screen, and moving it changes that run. The value you choose is also remembered across page reloads and is what each new run starts with; it survives Reset. The value each run actually used is recorded with that run and shown in the Run History 'Spr' column, so you can tell which runs are comparable with the dissertation's (100) and which are not. Controls which Slipnet nodes participate in activation spreading. Defaults to 100, which reproduces the original exactly: only fully-active nodes spread, matching the Scheme's `fully-active?` test against `%max-activation%` (100). Lowering it lets partially-active nodes spread too, each contributing in proportion to its own activation, which makes the Slipnet more diffuse and exploratory -- useful for experimenting, but no longer Metacat behaviour. Note this is a different cutoff from `%full-activation-threshold%` (50), which decides which nodes count as active for top-down codelet posting; the slider does not affect that.
- Eliza commentary: Toggles the narration style shown in the Commentary panel. On = friendly natural-language narration; off = technical descriptions.
- Breakpoint: Pause the run when the codelet count reaches a specific value. Useful for debugging or stepping through a specific point in a known run.

The status box at the bottom shows the current run number, total codelets executed so far, and the type of the most recently executed codelet.

title: Commentary
short_desc: Natural-language narration of what Metacat is doing and why, generated as the run unfolds.
full_desc:
The Commentary panel shows a running description of Metacat's cognitive activity during a run. Commentary is generated from the conceptual representations that Metacat builds -- it is not natural-language understanding, but template-based transcription of Slipnet concepts, built structures, discovered rules, and self-watching events into English prose.

Commentary has two modes, controlled by the 'Eliza commentary' checkbox in the Run Controls Settings group:

- Eliza mode (default): Friendly, narrative-style descriptions. For example: 'I notice abc has a successor pattern, and I'm looking at xyz to see if it has the same.' This mode makes runs easier to follow for new users and presentations.

- Technical mode: Precise, formal descriptions that name the specific structures and slippages involved. For example: 'Built successor-group bond between letters at positions 0 and 1 of initial-string.' This mode is useful for debugging and for users familiar with Metacat's internal vocabulary.

The commentary accumulates as new events happen: bonds built, groups formed, bridges made, rules discovered, snags encountered, answers found. Together with the Temporal Trace, it is the main way users observe what the engine is doing at a high level without having to read every codelet execution.

title: Run History
short_desc: A list of every recorded run in this Petacat instance, with quick links to load them back up. Fast runs are not recorded and do not appear.
full_desc:
The Run History panel shows all runs that have been created in the current Petacat instance, ordered by recency. Each entry shows the run number, problem strings (initial, modified, target, and answer if found), status (running, paused, halted, answer_found), final codelet count, and temperature.

Clicking a run entry loads that run's state back into the dashboard -- the Workspace, Slipnet, Coderack, Themespace, Trace, and other panels all refresh to show the selected run. The URL hash updates to '#/runs/N' so you can bookmark or share a direct link to any run.

What a run leaves behind here depends on the persistence mode it was created with. A Normal run has a row, its trace events, and a complete state capture at each of its two boundaries. An Audit run has all of that plus a log of every state-changing action. A Fast run has nothing at all -- it never touches the database, not even to insert the row that would list it, so it is absent from this panel by construction rather than by omission. Fast runs also take a negative run number, because there is no database row to take a positive one from.

A Fast run is listed from memory while it is loaded, with the status, codelet count, temperature and answer it holds, and is marked as unrecorded: it writes no row, so it is not available in Review and is gone from the list once another run takes its place.\n\nRun History is distinct from Episodic Memory: runs are database rows recording a particular problem-solving attempt, while episodic memory stores only the abstract answer and snag descriptions used for reminding. Deleting runs from the Admin panel clears this history; clearing episodic memory does not affect runs.

To look at what a Normal or Audit run recorded -- its start and end states, what changed between them, or a step-by-step walk through an audited run -- use the Review view in the hamburger menu rather than this panel. Clicking a run here reloads it into the live dashboard; Review reads the record instead.

title: Review
short_desc: Reads back what recorded runs wrote: a training session browser, a start-versus-end comparison for Normal runs, and a forward step-through for Audit runs.
full_desc:
The Review view is reached from the hamburger menu. Where the dashboard shows a run that is happening, Review shows runs that have already happened, rendered from what they recorded rather than from a live engine.

The left-hand panel lists training sessions, newest first, each expanding into the sequence of runs it contains with each run's persistence mode shown. Fast runs are not merely empty here -- they are absent, because a Fast run writes no database row at all. Selecting a run opens the review appropriate to its mode, since the two modes record genuinely different things and there is nothing sensible to show a reader who opens the wrong one.

**A Normal run** shows the complete state captured at its start, the complete state captured at its end, and a comparison of the two. The comparison is the useful part: the two captures are large and nearly identical, so rather than showing both it reports what actually moved -- how many codelets ran, how far the temperature fell, which structures were built in which string and which kinds of bridge were made, the rules the run finished holding together with their English descriptions, the largest changes in Slipnet activation, which themes moved and which were dominant at the end, and what the run contributed to the training session's episodic memory.

**An Audit run** gets a tick-by-tick inspector. Step forward through the run and see, at each tick, the codelet that ran, the structures that changed, and the activation and temperature at that instant. Stepping is forward-only in this release. The inspector works by restoring the run's start capture and walking a real engine forward, which is only honest if the reconstruction really is the recorded run -- so it is checked against the recorded action log as it goes.

Everything is drawn with the same Workspace, Slipnet, Themespace and Trace components as the live dashboard, pointed at recorded state instead of a running engine. One exception: the Slipnet graph is read-only here, because right-clicking a node clamps it and clamping a recording means nothing.

title: Configuration
short_desc: The thirteen collections that make up Petacat's domain knowledge, each on its own tab, each editable: create, update and delete rows and the next run created uses them.
full_desc:
The Configuration view is reached from the hamburger menu. Petacat keeps its domain knowledge in the database rather than in code -- the Slipnet's concepts and links, the codelet types and their Python bodies, the engine's parameters and formula coefficients, the theme dimensions, the posting rules, the codelet patterns, the commentary templates, the demo problems, the Slipnet grid layout and the help topics -- and this screen is where that knowledge is edited.

Thirteen collections, and every tab writes. Codelet patterns is the one without a tab of its own -- it is configured through the API and the seed file. The table-shaped ones -- slipnet nodes, slipnet links, urgency levels, formula coefficients, engine parameters, theme dimensions, posting rules, slipnet layout, demo problems and the enum tables -- edit in place: double-click a cell to change it, '+ Add' to create a row, and the cross at the end of a row to delete it, with a confirmation. A column holding a list or an object takes JSON, and a value that is not valid JSON is reported rather than sent. The two collections made of long text -- codelet types and help topics -- and the commentary templates each get a list beside an editor, so a codelet's execute_body, a topic's full description and a template's JSON have room to be worked on.

A refusal is reported where it happened and says what kind of problem it is: a name already taken, a value out of range, a row that is gone. A collection that fails to load says so and offers to try again, which reads differently from a collection that is empty.\n\nA saved change is picked up by the next run created. The run in progress keeps the configuration it started with, so an edit made mid-run takes effect on the run after it.

Two collection-wide operations sit alongside the tabs. 'Export Current Settings to Seed Data' writes the database's configuration back out to seed_data/*.json, which is how a configuration arrived at in the app becomes the project's starting point; each replaced file is copied first, under a timestamp, into seed_data/.backups/. The API's export and import routes carry the same thirteen collections as one JSON object, ordered by primary key, which makes a configuration backup diffable and restorable in a single transaction.

title: Clear Episodic Memory
short_desc: Removes all stored answer and snag descriptions from past runs.

user_description: Removes all stored answer descriptions and snag descriptions that Metacat has accumulated from past runs.
